source: Cycles on a P–V Diagram
Around a closed cycle ΔU = 0, and the area enclosed is the net work.
Students add up the work of each leg without signs, so the net work comes out as the whole area under the paths.

An engine cannot expand forever; it must come back to where it started and go again. A path on the P–V diagram that returns to its starting state is a cycle. Using the processes you know, we can do the bookkeeping for a whole cycle.

Internal energy belongs to the state. Back at the starting $P$ and $V$, the gas is back at its starting $T$ and $U$, so $\Delta U = 0$ around any cycle. Then the first law gives $Q_{\text{net}} = -W_{\text{net}}$: the net heat that flows in equals the net work the gas does. The gas does positive work while it expands and negative work while it is compressed; if it expands at a higher pressure than it is compressed at, the difference is the area inside the loop.

Around a cycle, $\Delta U = 0$ and $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{by}}$. The net work done by the gas equals the area enclosed: positive for a clockwise cycle (an engine), negative for a counterclockwise one (a refrigerator).
A rectangular cycle. The table lists $Q$, $W$ and $\Delta U$ for each leg; the $\Delta U$ column adds to zero.
Worked examples

A gas goes around A $(200\,\text{kPa}, 2.0\,\text{L})$ → B $(200\,\text{kPa}, 5.0\,\text{L})$ → C $(80\,\text{kPa}, 5.0\,\text{L})$ → D $(80\,\text{kPa}, 2.0\,\text{L})$ → A. Find the net work done by the gas.
Net work of a rectangle
$360\,\text{J}$ by the gas
A→B: expands at $200\,\text{kPa}$: $W_{\text{by}} = 200 \times 3.0 = +600\,\text{J}$.
B→C and D→A: constant volume, no work.
C→D: compressed at $80\,\text{kPa}$: $W_{\text{by}} = 80 \times (-3.0) = -240\,\text{J}$.
Net: $600 - 240 = 360\,\text{J}$, the enclosed area $(120\,\text{kPa})(3.0\,\text{L})$.
For a monatomic gas on the same cycle, find $Q$ for each leg and check the totals.
Bookkeeping the legs
Use $\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(PV)$ and $Q = \Delta U - W$, with $W$ on the gas.
Totals: $\Delta U = 0$, $W = -360\,\text{J}$, $Q = 1500 - 900 - 600 + 360 = 360\,\text{J}$. The net heat equals the net work by the gas.

A gas goes from $(100\,\text{kPa}, 1.0\,\text{L})$ up to $(300\,\text{kPa}, 1.0\,\text{L})$, along a straight line to $(100\,\text{kPa}, 4.0\,\text{L})$, and back at constant pressure. Find the net work by the gas.
A triangle
The cycle runs clockwise, so the net work by the gas is the enclosed area, positive.

Adding up the work of each leg without signs, which gives the whole area under the paths ($600 + 240 = 840\,\text{J}$ above) instead of the area enclosed ($360\,\text{J}$). Expansion and compression have opposite signs. Check: the net work can never be more than the area inside the loop.
